kernelNetworking: Home Kernel / Networking Kconfig Kconfig · built-in vs module, symbol by symbol Kernel networking: what goes in, what gets loaded Every networking failure that begins with "operation not supported" is usually a symbol set to the wrong letter years earlier. This page explains the three markers in make menuconfig , gives the rule that decides built-in versus module, and then walks the networking menu option by option — routing tables, netfilter, bridges, tunnels, traffic control and eBPF — so the choice is a reason, not a reflex. <*> vs <M> policy routing netfilter + nftables tc / XDP 01 The markers, and what (*) really is The notation is the first thing tutorials blur. There is no (*) symbol in the kernel config; menuconfig draws three different markers, and confusing them is how people "enable routing" by ticking a boolean that only controls whether a module is even offered. You see Symbol type Means Can be unloaded? <*> tristate, value y Compiled into the kernel image No <M> tristate, value m Compiled as a separate .ko Yes, unless in use < > tristate, value n Not built at all — [*] boolean On or off only; there is no module form No {M} / {*} forced Selected by another option you enabled Only by disabling the parent That table answers half the question by itself: many routing features are booleans , so they show as [*] and cannot be modules at all. Where a symbol is a tristate, the decision is real. The rule that decides everything Build in what the machine needs before it can load modules ; make everything else a module. In practice: storage, console, the NIC the initramfs brings up, and anything the initramfs needs to reach the root filesystem. Networking beyond that is almost always a module — unless you intend to burn the bridge by disabling module loading. 02 Where the truth lives Never trust a blog for a symbol name — including this one. The kernel tree names its own symbols, and the running kernel can tell you what it was built with. # what am I running, and was this config even exposed? uname -r zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "CONFIG_(IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES|NF_CONNTRACK)=" ls /boot/config-"$(uname -r)" # the authoritative definition, in the source tree grep -n "config IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES" -A 12 net/ipv4/Kconfig scripts/config --file .config --state CONFIG_BRIDGE # change the config without menuconfig scripts/config --file .config --module BRIDGE make olddefconfig # resolve new symbols with defaults scripts/diffconfig .config.old .config # exactly what you changed localmodconfig is tempting — it keeps only the modules currently loaded. It is fine for a laptop, and a trap for a router: the modules your firewall needs may simply not be loaded on the build machine when you run it. 03 What must be built in Symbol Why it cannot be a module here VIRTIO_NET Cloud and VM images whose root disk is virtual need the NIC before root mounts E1000E , IGB , IXGBE The physical port used for PXE, NFS root or iSCSI boot BRIDGE Only if the root filesystem is behind a bridge (rare) or modules are disabled VLAN_8021Q When the management interface is tagged and configured in the initramfs BONDING When the boot interface is a bond PACKET If the machine's only diagnostic is tcpdump on a rescue image with no modules Everything else on this page is a module in a sane configuration. The price of =y is permanent memory and a permanently larger trusted computing base; the price of =m is a load step and the risk that the module is not there after a kernel upgrade. 04 Routing and policy routing # Networking support -> Networking options CONFIG_NET=y # [*] the whole stack CONFIG_INET=y # [*] TCP/IP CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER=y # [*] unlocks the routing extras below CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] ip rule, policy routing CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH=y # [*] several nexthops per route CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_CLASSID=y # [*] tc classification by route CONFIG_IPV6_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] the same for IPv6 CONFIG_IPV6_SUBTREES=y # [*] source-based IPv6 lookups Symbol Form Turn it on when IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER bool [*] Always on a router or firewall; it gates the rest IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES bool [*] You use ip rule , VRFs, or anything with multiple routing tables IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH bool [*] Two uplinks, or the ECMP lab from the GNS3 page IP_ROUTE_CLASSID bool [*] Traffic control keyed on a route class IPV6 tristate You have IPv6 — build in if the address is assigned before modules load These are booleans, so "make it a module" is not an option and the question becomes whether to enable them at all. A kernel without IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES still routes; it just ignores every second table, and ip rule commands appear to succeed while doing nothing. 05 Netfilter, conntrack, NAT # core: everything else depends on these CONFIG_NETFILTER=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=m <M> the state table CONFIG_NF_NAT=m <M> NAT engine, needed by MASQUERADE CONFIG_NF_TABLES=m <M> the nftables core CONFIG_NF_TABLES_INET=m <M> one table for v4 and v6 CONFIG_NFT_CT=m <M> ct expression CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES=m <M> the xtables compatibility layer CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_MASQUERADE=m CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_FTP=m # helpers: load only what you need Symbol Form Effect if missing NF_CONNTRACK tristate No stateful rules, no NAT, no conntrack tool NF_NAT tristate MASQUERADE and DNAT simply do not exist NF_TABLES tristate nft reports no such file or unsupported NETFILTER_XTABLES tristate Legacy iptables rules fail to apply NF_CONNTRACK_FTP etc. tristate Only that protocol's helper is absent — good default Modules are fine here — until you disable modules Debian and every mainstream distro ship netfilter as modules, and it works. Build it in when you plan to set kernel.modules_disabled=1 after boot, or when the firewall must be able to drop packets before any userspace process has run. 06 Bridges, VLANs, bonds, virtual links Symbol Recommended Needed by BRIDGE <M> Anything that bridges: VMs, containers, the GNS3 switch BRIDGE_NETFILTER <M> iptables on bridged traffic; Docker needs it VLAN_8021Q <M> ip link add ... type vlan BONDING <M> LACP and failover bonds MACVLAN / IPVLAN <M> Many addresses on one NIC, container networking VETH <M> Namespaces, containers, test topologies DUMMY <M> A stable interface that stays up with no cable IFB <M> Ingress shaping — redirecting ingress into a qdisc TUN <M> VPNs and user-space tunnels; also creates tap These are cheap modules and there is no security reason to build them in. The one exception is a host that cannot load modules at all, where every link type the boot scripts create must be present in the image. 07 Tunnels and VPNs Symbol Recommended Note WIREGUARD <M> One module, no dependencies; "Unknown device type" means it is missing VXLAN <M> Overlay networks; needs a UDP tunnel port GENEVE <M> The newer overlay encapsulation NET_IPIP <M> Simple IPv4-in-IPv4 NET_IPGRE <M> GRE, including the keyed form IPV6_SIT <M> IPv6 in IPv4, legacy but still used XFRM_USER , INET_ESP <M> IPsec; the user interface plus the ESP transform INET_AH <M> Authentication header, rarely the right choice today Tunnels are the classic "loads on demand" case: the interface type is requested by name from userspace, and the kernel autoloads the module. If autoloading is disabled, the module has to be in the image or loaded explicitly at boot. 08 Traffic control and eBPF CONFIG_NET_SCHED=y CONFIG_NET_SCH_HTB=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_CAKE=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_FQ_CODEL=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_INGRESS=m # the hook for clsact CONFIG_NET_CLS_ACT=y # [*] actions are not optional once you classify CONFIG_NET_ACT_MIRRED=m # redirect: ingress shaping, mirroring CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER=m # hardware-offloadable matching CONFIG_NET_CLS_U32=m CONFIG_NET_CLS_BPF=m CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL=y # [*] required by every eBPF tool CONFIG_BPF_JIT=y CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF=y # [*] libbpf CO-RE needs this NET_SCHED and BPF_SYSCALL are booleans; the qdiscs and classifiers are modules. A "qdisc not found" error is a missing sch_*.ko , while "Operation not supported" on a flower filter is a missing cls_flower.ko — two different messages, two different symbols. XDP is a driver property, not just a config option eBPF itself is in the core, but XDP offload needs driver support and, for the native path, a driver that implements it. On veth and tun you get the generic path; on a card that does not support it, the program simply will not attach natively. 09 Sockets that let you see Symbol Recommended Tool that breaks without it PACKET <M> tcpdump , Snort afpacket, Suricata INET_DIAG <M> ss , socket listings in monitoring agents INET_TCP_DIAG , INET_UDP_DIAG <M> Per-protocol detail for ss -t / -u UNIX_DIAG <M> ss -x NETLINK_DIAG <M> Netlink socket inspection IKCONFIG + IKCONFIG_PROC [*] /proc/config.gz — without it, no way to audit the build IKCONFIG is the cheapest hardening decision on this page: it embeds the config so anyone can check what was built, including you, two years later. Hide it if the config itself is sensitive; keep it if you would rather be auditable. 10 Options that harden by removing CONFIG_MODULE_SIG=y CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE=y # refuse unsigned modules entirely CONFIG_MODULE_UNLOAD=n # nothing can be unloaded CONFIG_KEXEC=n CONFIG_STRICT_KERNEL_RWX=y CONFIG_DEBUG_WX=y # runtime, after everything is loaded sysctl -w kernel.modules_disabled=1 MODULE_SIG_FORCE makes every module signed and trusted; a third-party driver you built yourself needs a key in the kernel keyring. MODULE_UNLOAD=n removes the ability to replace a loaded module — and the ability to recover from a bad one without rebooting. modules_disabled=1 is the strongest and least reversible: after it, no module loads. Everything the machine will ever need must already be loaded or built in. Do the arithmetic before the reboot A router that disables modules at boot must have bridging, VLAN, conntrack and the firewall built in — and the tests on this page run before the setting is permanent. The usual outcome of doing it in the other order is a machine that powers on and never passes a packet again. 11 Three role fragments These are starting points for make olddefconfig , not gospel: symbol names and defaults move between versions, and your hardware decides the driver lines. # A. Router / firewall (Debian, netfilter as modules) CONFIG_NET=y CONFIG_INET=y CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER=y CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH=y CONFIG_NETFILTER=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=m CONFIG_NF_NAT=m CONFIG_NF_TABLES=m CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES=m CONFIG_BRIDGE=m CONFIG_VLAN_8021Q=m # B. Virtualisation host (everything a guest might ask for) CONFIG_BRIDGE=m CONFIG_BRIDGE_NETFILTER=m CONFIG_VETH=m CONFIG_TUN=m CONFIG_MACVLAN=m CONFIG_VXLAN=m CONFIG_OPENVSWITCH=m # C. Hardened appliance (modules disabled after boot) CONFIG_VIRTIO_NET=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=y CONFIG_NF_NAT=y CONFIG_NF_TABLES=y CONFIG_IP_NF_IPTABLES=y CONFIG_BRIDGE=y CONFIG_PACKET=y CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE=y CONFIG_IKCONFIG=y CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC=y The pattern is visible: same features, different letter. A is the mainstream choice and the easiest to maintain; C is the one you can reason about at the packet level, at the cost of never being able to add a feature without a rebuild. 12 Prove the build # what is actually in this kernel zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES|NF_CONNTRACK|BRIDGE|PACKET" lsmod | grep -E "nf_|bridge|vlan" # each subsystem, asked the only way that counts ip rule add fwmark 1 table 100; ip rule show # policy routing nft list tables # nftables iptables -t nat -L -n | head -3 # legacy NAT table tc qdisc show dev lo # traffic control ip link add vtest type veth peer name vtest2 # veth tcpdump -i any -c1 -w /dev/null 2>&1 # AF_PACKET conntrack -L 2>/dev/null | wc -l # state table ss -s # socket diag Check Good sign What a failure tells you ip rule add Rule listed IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES off — the rule "works" but is ignored nft list tables Empty list, no error NF_TABLES missing iptables -t nat Table prints NF_NAT or xtables missing tcpdump One packet captured PACKET missing: every sensor on the box is blind ip link add veth Pair created VETH missing Run the same set after every kernel upgrade. The build you audited is not the build that boots tomorrow — check the external references for the current symbol names when the output disagrees with the page. 13 Failure table Symptom Missing symbol Fix tcpdump: socket: Address family not supported PACKET <M> and load af_packet iptables: Table does not exist NF_NAT / IP_NF_NAT Enable NAT, reload the firewall nft: no such file or directory NF_TABLES Build the nftables core, not just xtables A rule in table 100 is ignored IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES Boolean: rebuild required RTNETLINK answers: Operation not supported on a filter NET_CLS_FLOWER Load the classifier module Unknown device type for wg0 WIREGUARD Module, not a userspace package iptables rules never see bridged frames BRIDGE_NETFILTER Enable, then check br_netfilter is loaded Works until reboot after an upgrade Running kernel ≠ /lib/modules Reboot into the new image, or pin the kernel A module cannot be loaded at all MODULE_SIG_FORCE or modules_disabled Sign it, or rebuild everything in 14 Sources Kernel networking — the authoritative documentation for routing, netfilter and tc. Debian security Networking Snort Início Kernel / Kconfig de rede Kconfig · built-in ou módulo, símbolo a símbolo Rede no kernel: o que entra na imagem e o que é carregado Quase todas as falhas de rede que começam com «operation not supported» são um símbolo com a letra errada, escolhida anos antes. Esta página explica os três marcadores do make menuconfig , dá a regra que decide entre built-in e módulo e percorre o menu de rede opção a opção — tabelas de rotas, netfilter, bridges, túneis, controlo de tráfego e eBPF — para a escolha ser uma razão e não um reflexo. <*> vs <M> rotas por política netfilter + nftables tc / XDP 01 Os marcadores e o que é (*) A notação é a primeira coisa que os tutoriais baralham. Não existe um símbolo (*) na configuração do kernel: o menuconfig desenha três marcadores diferentes, e confundi-los é como alguém «ativa o encaminhamento» carregando num booleano que só controla se um módulo é sequer oferecido. Vê Tipo de símbolo Significa Pode descarregar? <*> tristate, valor y Compilado dentro da imagem do kernel Não <M> tristate, valor m Compilado como .ko separado Sim, se não estiver em uso < > tristate, valor n Não é compilado de todo — [*] booleano Só ligado ou desligado; não há forma de módulo Não {M} / {*} forçado Selecionado por outra opção que ativou Só desativando o pai Essa tabela responde a metade da pergunta: muitas funcionalidades de encaminhamento são booleanas , aparecem como [*] e não podem ser módulos. Onde o símbolo é tristate, a decisão é real. A regra que decide tudo Compile dentro o que a máquina precisa antes de conseguir carregar módulos ; o resto é módulo. Na prática: armazenamento, consola, a NIC que o initramfs levanta e tudo o que o initramfs precisa para chegar à raiz. Rede para além disso é quase sempre módulo — a menos que pretenda desativar o carregamento de módulos de vez. 02 Onde está a verdade Nunca confie num blog para um nome de símbolo — incluindo este. A árvore do kernel nomeia os seus símbolos, e o kernel em execução sabe com o que foi compilado. # o que estou a correr, e a configuração foi exposta? uname -r zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "CONFIG_(IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES|NF_CONNTRACK)=" ls /boot/config-"$(uname -r)" # a definição autoritária, na árvore de código grep -n "config IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES" -A 12 net/ipv4/Kconfig scripts/config --file .config --state CONFIG_BRIDGE # mudar a configuração sem menuconfig scripts/config --file .config --module BRIDGE make olddefconfig # resolver símbolos novos com omissões scripts/diffconfig .config.old .config # exatamente o que mudou localmodconfig é tentador — mantém só os módulos carregados. Serve para um portátil e é uma armadilha para um router: os módulos de que a firewall precisa podem simplesmente não estar carregados na máquina de compilação quando o corre. 03 O que tem de ser built-in Símbolo Porque não pode ser módulo aqui VIRTIO_NET Imagens de cloud e VM com disco virtual precisam da NIC antes da raiz montar E1000E , IGB , IXGBE A porta física usada para PXE, raiz NFS ou boot iSCSI BRIDGE Só se a raiz estiver atrás de uma bridge (raro) ou com módulos desativados VLAN_8021Q Quando a interface de gestão é etiquetada e configurada no initramfs BONDING Quando a interface de arranque é um bond PACKET Se o único diagnóstico da máquina é tcpdump numa imagem de resgate sem módulos Todo o resto desta página é módulo numa configuração sensata. O preço de =y é memória permanente e uma base de confiança maior; o preço de =m é um passo de carregamento e o risco de o módulo não existir depois de uma atualização do kernel. 04 Rotas e rotas por política # Networking support -> Networking options CONFIG_NET=y # [*] a pilha inteira CONFIG_INET=y # [*] TCP/IP CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER=y # [*] destranca o resto abaixo CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] ip rule, rotas por política CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH=y # [*] vários nexthops por rota CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_CLASSID=y # [*] classificação tc pela rota CONFIG_IPV6_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] o mesmo para IPv6 CONFIG_IPV6_SUBTREES=y # [*] procuras IPv6 por origem Símbolo Forma Ativar quando IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER bool [*] Sempre num router ou firewall; abre caminho ao resto IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES bool [*] Usa ip rule , VRFs ou várias tabelas IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH bool [*] Dois uplinks, ou o ECMP do laboratório GNS3 IP_ROUTE_CLASSID bool [*] Controlo de tráfego indexado a uma classe de rota IPV6 tristate Tem IPv6 — built-in se o endereço é atribuído antes dos módulos São booleanos, portanto «fazer disto um módulo» não é opção e a pergunta passa a ser se os ativar de todo. Um kernel sem IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES continua a encaminhar; apenas ignora todas as tabelas secundárias, e os comandos ip rule parecem funcionar sem fazer nada. 05 Netfilter, conntrack, NAT # núcleo: tudo o resto depende disto CONFIG_NETFILTER=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=m <M> a tabela de estados CONFIG_NF_NAT=m <M> motor NAT, necessário ao MASQUERADE CONFIG_NF_TABLES=m <M> o núcleo do nftables CONFIG_NF_TABLES_INET=m <M> uma tabela para v4 e v6 CONFIG_NFT_CT=m <M> expressão ct CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES=m <M> camada de compatibilidade xtables CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_MASQUERADE=m CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_FTP=m # helpers: carregar só o necessário Símbolo Forma Efeito se faltar NF_CONNTRACK tristate Sem regras com estado, sem NAT, sem ferramenta conntrack NF_NAT tristate MASQUERADE e DNAT simplesmente não existem NF_TABLES tristate nft responde que não existe ou não é suportado NETFILTER_XTABLES tristate Regras iptables legadas falham ao aplicar NF_CONNTRACK_FTP etc. tristate Só falta o helper desse protocolo — bom padrão Módulos servem — até desativar módulos Debian e todas as distribuições principais trazem o netfilter como módulos, e funciona. Compile dentro quando pretende pôr kernel.modules_disabled=1 depois do arranque, ou quando a firewall tem de poder descartar pacotes antes de qualquer processo de utilizador correr. 06 Bridges, VLANs, bonds, links virtuais Símbolo Recomendado Necessário para BRIDGE <M> Tudo o que faz bridge: VMs, contentores, o switch do GNS3 BRIDGE_NETFILTER <M> iptables em tráfego comutado; o Docker precisa VLAN_8021Q <M> ip link add ... type vlan BONDING <M> Bonds LACP e de failover MACVLAN / IPVLAN <M> Muitos endereços numa NIC, rede de contentores VETH <M> Nam

kingdomOfTUIs: Terminal Handbook · Application Atlas Kingdom of TUIs A terminal user interface is a program that owns the screen of your terminal and behaves like an application: a file manager with panels, a monitor with graphs, a Git client with staging, a database browser. No window manager, no mouse required, no browser engine — just cells, keys and colour. This page is a field guide to the applications you can actually install on Linux today, with their GitHub projects, so you can jump straight to the source and the README. Everything below runs inside a plain terminal on Linux. Most are single binaries or small packages; a few need a helper service (music players that speak MPD, for example). The lists are organised by what you are trying to get done, not by language or framework, because that is how you will look for them. If a project is marked popular , it is one of the ones with the largest GitHub communities — a proxy for documentation, issues answered, and years of bug reports. All File managers 9 Yazi popular Async file manager in Rust with image, video and archive previews. Extremely fast on huge directories and pleasant to theme. Rust · Linux, macOS ranger The classic three-column, vi-inspired file manager. Python, previews, bookmarks, and a plugin ecosystem that has aged well. Python · Linux, macOS, BSD lf Ranger's spirit written in Go: one binary, configurable keybindings, shell integration, and no Python runtime to carry around. Go · Linux, macOS, BSD nnn Very small C file manager with a plugin system, session handling and batch operations. The one to install on a rescue system. C · Linux, macOS, BSD Vifm Dual-pane file manager with genuine Vim keybindings, registers and a command line. Feels like editing a filesystem. C · Linux, macOS, BSD broot Not a manager but a navigator: fuzzy search across the tree, preview panels, and a language for composing filesystem queries. knowledgeLabyrinth: Mind · Machine · Archive God(道) Descent Knowledge Labyrinth labyrinthus Not a maze to get lost in — a descent with the lights on. Twelve layers, from the instrument in your hand to the exit condition, every wall labelled and every claim carrying a receipt. MindOS, permission lattices, kernel diffs, regression, provenance — and the psychology of anyone, this author included, who mistakes a map for the ground. OdicforceSounds Monkey Blog Technical Edition Mixed With Reality Mind · Machine · Archive — always layered Layer 0 Threshold The Entry Is Already a Model Before the first wall, the instrument. Before you enter the labyrinth, notice the instrument you are using to enter it. A browser, a reader, a terminal, a mind — each is a model of the world with its own permission lattice, its own defaults, its own hidden assumptions about what can be seen and what can be done. The labyrinth does not begin where the first wall appears. It begins where the first model is applied. That is why the first layer is always the hardest to see: you are using it to look at everything else. ⌘ Model First ◈ See the Lens ◉ Reality Has Layers "A map is not the territory, but a bad map will make you walk off the edge and call it progress." Layer 1 Map Two Maps: Territory and Procedure The labyrinth is a place and a method. There are at least two things a labyrinth can mean. One is a territory : a space of possible states, paths, dead ends, and re-entries. Knowledge, risk, identity, law, power, code — each can be drawn as a topology and then walked. The other is a procedure : a set of moves, checks, proofs, tests, audits, decisions. The labyrinth here is not a place you are lost in; it is a sequence of constraints you satisfy or fail. Both maps are real. The error is to confuse which one you are holding. Confusion What it looks like Territory mistaken for procedure You think you are walking a real space, but you are only following rules that may not fit the ground. Procedure mistaken for territory You think you are obeying a method, but you are actually wandering without one and calling it exploration. Science without procedure You claim a fact while ignoring measurement, sampling, and falsifiability. Psychology without territory You name a feeling without checking what in the world actually triggers it. "The Monkey does not choose one map. The Monkey keeps both visible and switches deliberately." Layer 2 Kinds of Real What Kind of "Real" Are We Talking About? Not one stamp. Several lenses. "Real" is not a single stamp you can put on a thing and be done. There are at least these kinds, and they behave differently under pressure: Layer What it means Tag Nominal A thing with a name and a contract around the name. Label Observed A thing inferred from repeatable measurements. Science Regulatory A thing defined by rules, jurisdiction, and enforcement. Law Structural A thing whose role is defined by how it connects, not by what it is called. Graph Operational A thing that behaves a certain way when pressure is applied. Stress Provenancial A thing whose reality is tied to its line of descent, edits, receipts, and witnesses. Trace Psychological A thing real to the organism because it shapes perception, memory, fear, and action. Mind A labyrinth made of only one kind of "real" is usually a trap dressed as depth. The Monkey prefers multi-layered: name, measurement, rule, structure, behavior, provenance, and the felt reality of a nervous system — and a clear label on which layer you are currently debating. Layer 3 MindOS Architecture of a Mind-OS A working hypothesis with visible parts. A "MindOS" is a name for a working hypothesis: an internal system that coordinates perception, memory, action, inhibition, and revision. It is not necessarily a thing you can point to and hold; it is a thing you can point to by its effects and constraints. Useful descriptions of such a system usually include, at minimum: ◈ Input Filters ◉ State ⚙ Action Selection ⊡ Inhibition ↻ Revision ⌛ Provenance MindOS — working schema Input filters what gets admitted, ignored, or flagged for later State representation what is active, dormant, or evicted right now Action selection how one candidate behavior is chosen over another Inhibition what is suppressed, and by what authority Revision when and how the system updates its own model Provenance and memory what is kept, for how long, and in what form The interesting failures are rarely "the system is not smart enough." They are usually more specific: the filters were too narrow, the state was wrong, the inhibition was too strong or too weak, the revision was too late, or the provenance was missing when it mattered. "An operating system is not wise. It is consistent under pressure — or it is not." Layer 4 Activation Activation Maps Where activity concentrates, and why. If you look at a maze from enough distance, you do not see walls first. You see flow . In a nervous system, in a network, in a body of documents, in a political field, in a person's habits — there are regions where activity clusters, and regions where it is suppressed. Call them activation maps if you want a name. The name matters less than the observability. Activation maps are interesting because they reveal structure without needing a grand theory to explain it first: Where does attention repeatedly return? Where does it fail to return even when it should? Where does activity move quickly, and where does it stall? What suppresses it — internal rules, external force, fatigue, fear, design, reward? Do not confuse "active" with "true" and do not confuse "quiet" with "unimportant." Silence can be a dead end, but it can also be a bottleneck, a concealment, or a place where the wrong thing was removed from the map on purpose. "A quiet region is not always empty. Sometimes it is policed." Layer 5 Permissions Permissions and Borders A lattice, not a wall. Borders are often drawn as lines. A better model is a lattice: many points, many relations, and many possible paths between them, some allowed, some denied, some conditional. In a system with any seriousness, permissions are not one gate. They are a lattice of decisions: R Read W Write X Execute D Delegate N Deny A Audit V Revoke Permission If missing, what breaks Read You can act without seeing what you are acting on. Write The system can be steered by whoever can alter state. Execute Intent can remain inert if it cannot be run. Delegate Authority cannot scale without it, and bottlenecks grow. Deny Without explicit denial, exception becomes the rule. Audit Without audit, permission is only a claim. Revoke Without revocation, a lost edge can stay live for too long. "A wall is what you see. A lattice is what you must walk." Layer 6 BSD Lattice On the BSD Permission Lattice A small lattice, seriously studied. Unix file modes are a small but instructive example. They are not "ownership" in any grand sense; they are a lattice of execute, write, and read rights across three classes of actor — owner, group, other — plus a few metadata flags that change how the lattice behaves in practice. The form is compact. The lessons are not: Read, write, execute are not interchangeable abstractions. Each changes the character of access in a different way. Owner/group/other are a coarse social boundary. Coarse boundaries are cheap to think about and expensive to rely on when the world is finer than the model. Setuid/setgid/sticky are not decoration. They change the effective lattice by introducing transitions and constraints that can invert who is really in control at runtime. A permission model that is "mostly right" can still be attacked through the few places where the lattice is under-specified. Study it as a toy model of a deeper problem: access is not a single bit. It is a structure of transitions, and transitions are where surprises live. Permission lattice — coarse example Class r w x real meaning Owner read write exec the named owner Group read write exec membership edge Other read write exec everyone else Layer 7 Audit Audit and the Kernel Diff What can be checked when pressure is applied. A labyrinth is not just a structure. It is a structure plus the ability to detect when it has been altered. That is the role of audit. Without audit, "permission" is a claim. With audit, it becomes a traceable decision, or at least an attempt at one. A kernel diff is one kind of trace: a record that something changed, where, and under which conditions of authority. The hard part is not producing a diff. The hard part is making the diff meaningful when the thing being changed is itself the authority that decides what counts as a valid diff. That is why serious systems think in layers again: what changed who was able to change it what that change enables next who can see the change happened who can challenge it what can revert it what can prove it was or was not reverted If any one of those is missing, the labyrinth has a blind corridor. "A change with no receipt is a claim with no spine." Layer 8 Regression Regression and Provenance The maze must be able to remember. A labyrinth that cannot say what it was yesterday is not a labyrinth worth trusting. Regression is the warning that a later state may be worse in a way that is not obvious from the immediate change. Provenance is the record that lets you ask where a state came from, which choices led to it, and which constraints were in force at the time. These two ideas belong together because they fight different failures: Concern Question it asks Tag Regression did we lose something we previously had, even if the new thing looks better on one axis? Test Provenance can we reconstruct the path that led here, and does that record survive the next change? Receipt Psychological regression does the organism revert under stress to an older, narrower response? Stress Scientific regression does the later result still survive in a broader sample or a harder test? Replicate Without regression awareness, progress becomes a one-way ratchet that may be driving you into a corner. Without provenance, responsibility becomes a fog and accountability becomes a performance. Layer 9 Descent How Descent Actually Works Go down by choice, not by accident. A labyrinth can feel like descent if you wander into it. That is the cheap version. The technical version is different: descent is deliberate, and it is tracked. Real descent has properties: You know what layer you are on, at least approximately. You know what you are giving up to go deeper. You know what would count as coming back up. You leave a trace that is readable by the standards of the layer you left, not the layer you entered. You do not confuse depth with truth, nor novelty with insight. This is where the Monkey differs from the brute. The brute wants the deep thing because it is deep. The Monkey wants the deep thing because it is auditable , repeatable , and capable of failing in a way that teaches something . ↓ Deliberate ⌛ Tracked ↩ Reversible ◉ Real Layer 10 Exit The Exit Condition Exit is also a map. If you only think about entering, you will eventually be surprised by the exit problem: what does it mean to leave this labyrinth with something real? A good exit is not "I got out." A good exit is "I can show what I carried, what I changed, what I could not verify, and where the next blind corridor is." That is the difference between exploration and tourism. Tourism wants the story of having been there. Exploration wants the map, the receipt, and the next question. "If you descend without a trace, you did not descend. You disappeared." Layer 11 Monkey The Monkey's Way Hold the opposites, keep the trace. The Monkey does not prefer the territory to the procedure, or the procedure to the territory. The Monkey prefers to be able to name which one is being used at each step. That is the deeper technical discipline here: not "more depth," but better labelling of depth . MindOS, activation maps, permission lattice, audit, kernel diff, regression, provenance — these are not decorations. They are the tools that keep descent from becoming mystification. If you want the labyrinth to be real, do not make it prettier. Make it more checkable. Make it easier to enter and leave with something you can stand behind. Make it possible to tell, after the fact, whether the walls moved or only the walker did. That is the Monkey's technical ethic. Not clean. Not simple. But traceable. ◈ Checkable ◉ Mixed ⚙ Operational ⌛ Provenanced Traceable Descent Keep the Map, Keep the Receipt Descent is not a trick. It is a discipline: model, observe, constrain, audit, remember. If you lose the map, you are not exploring. If you lose the receipt, you are not learning. If you lose both, you are just moving. ← Back Top The Monkey O Macaco Path & Dream

learnHacking: How Hacking Happens — And How To Stop It Blue team to understand attack paths. Red team to break them. Lab only. No real targets without written permission. Ever. Ethics first — read or close this file: Only hack systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test (your lab, CTF, bug-bounty scope). Unauthorized access, credential cracking against real accounts, malware, ransomware, doxxing = crimes. This manual teaches concepts + defense + lab practice , not how to break into real systems. If in doubt, defend. 0 — Map: Hats, Teams, Bounties White hat: authorized defender/researcher. Black hat: criminal. Gray hat: unauthorized but claims good intent — still illegal, don't. Red team: authorized adversary emulation. Blue team: detect/respond/harden. Purple: both collaborate. Bug bounty: legal hacking inside a scope + rules (see HackerOne , Bugcrowd , GitHub Security Lab ). Start with OWASP Top 10 + OWASP Testing Guide . Papers to read (defensive lens): NIST SP 800 series (800-53, 800-115 testing) , MITRE ATT&CK (adversary tactics map), Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed), NIST Incident Handling 800-61 . 1 — Lab, Not Real Life: Isolate Your Experiments Build a lab you can break without breaking law or others: Host: Debian/Ubuntu, updated, firewall on Hypervisor: VirtualBox (https://www.virtualbox.org/) or KVM/QEMU + virt-manager Net: Host-only / NAT, NO bridge to home LAN for vulnerable VMs Targets (vulnerable-by-design, local only): - Metasploitable 2/3 (https://github.com/rapid7/metasploitable3) - OWASP Juice Shop (https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop) - DVWA (https://github.com/digininja/DVWA) - WebGoat (https://github.com/WebGoat/WebGoat) Attacker: Kali Linux (https://www.kali.org/) as a toolbox, snapshots before/after Capture: Wireshark (https://www.wireshark.org/) on host-only only Snapshot everything. Lab firewall: vulnerable VMs must never reach internet. No real credentials, no real data, no scanning outside 192.168.56.0/24 lab range. Secure your lab: separate user, encrypted disk ( LUKS docs ), ufw deny incoming on host, VPN kill-switch if you must fetch tools, GPG-verify ISOs. 2 — How Attacks Are Structured (Kill Chain → ATT&CK, Defensive View) Recon → weaponize → deliver → exploit → install → command → act. Map each to ATT&CK tactics. Blue counters: harden, detect, segment, log, respond. Example: phishing (Initial Access) fails if MFA + user training + mail filtering win. Study NIST CSF : Govern/Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover. 3 — Recon & Scanning: What Attackers See, How Defenders Shrink It Concept: DNS, subdomains, ports, services, versions leak attack surface. Tools defenders use to audit own scope: Nmap ( nmap.org , github/nmap ), Amass ( owasp-amass ), theHarvester ( theHarvester ), Shodan ( shodan.io — defender search for own exposure). # LAB ONLY against your own VMs, e.g. 192.168.56.101: nmap -sV -O 192.168.56.101 # versions, OS guess — then YOU patch/hide them # Blue: close ports, least service, banner minimization, WAF/CDN in front Blue lesson: every open port/version you see, attacker sees. Inventory with Nmap , then firewall, update, segment. Log scans with Suricata / Snort . 4 — Web: The #1 Real-World Path (Understand → Fix) Learn OWASP Top 10 : injection, broken access control, XSS, SSRF, misconfig. Practice defensively on Juice Shop / DVWA locally; intercept with Burp Suite Community ( portswigger ) or OWASP ZAP ( zaproxy , github ). Defense pattern (the point): parameterize queries, ORM, allow-list validation ( Zod ), output-encode, CSP + HttpOnly/SameSite cookies via Helmet ( helmetjs ), strict access checks server-side, SSRF allow-lists + no cloud metadata access. Scan own code with Semgrep , deps with Grype . 5 — C Fundamentals: Stack, Memory, Why Safe Code Matters You don't need to exploit to defend — but you must grasp why memory bugs are critical. Theory only, lab only: // stack frame (simplified x86-64): high -> low // [args][ret addr][saved rbp][locals: char buf[64]] // Unsafe copy can overflow locals -> crash/hijack in theory. // Defense: -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -Wl,-z,RelRO,-z,Now -fPIE -pie // + ASLR, NX, canaries, fuzzing, modern langs (Rust/Go) for new code. Learn safely: RPISEC MBE (course), pwn.college (ASU, lab + defense), awesome-pwn (curated learning) , papers: Smashing the Stack (Phrack 49, historic) — read as history + why mitigations exist. Practice defense: compile with protections, run ASan/UBSan , fuzz with AFL++ on your own code, verify with checksec / hardening-check . 6 — Passwords/Cracking: Why We Harden Auth (No Real Cracking) Concept: weak/reused passwords + no MFA = breach. Attackers use leaked lists + guessing in theory; your job is to make it fail : long unique passwords in KeePassXC ( keepassxc.org ), MFA everywhere (TOTP/WebAuthn), bcrypt/argon2 server-side, rate-limit + lockout, breach monitoring ( HIBP ). Audit own hashes in lab only with John ( openwall ) / Hashcat ( hashcat ) docs to prove policy works — never against others. 7 — Blue Team: Detect, Log, Respond Tools: Wireshark ( wireshark ) for packets, Suricata / Snort IDS, Wazuh ( wazuh , github ) SIEM, TheHive+Cortex ( TheHive ) case mgmt, Velociraptor ( velociraptor ) DFIR, Ghidra ( ghidra , NSA github ) for malware analysis in isolated VM . Playbooks: NIST 800-61 , SANS whitepapers . Log centrally, time-sync (NTP), alert on ATT&CK techniques you actually see in lab, rehearse restore from offline backups. Blue wins by preparation, not heroics. 8 — Bug Bounty Path (Legal Hacking Career) 1) Learn web + networking basics. 2) Lab: Juice Shop → PortSwigger Academy ( portswigger academy ). 3) Read scopes twice, respect out-of-scope, rate limits, disclosure rules. 4) Report: repro, impact, fix. Repos: OWASP WSTG checklist , HackTricks (defensive reference — use on own scope only) , PayloadsAllTheThings (test payloads for own lab/scope) . Never extort, never pivot beyond scope, never access real user data. 9 — Study Plan (6 Weeks, Lab + Defense) W1 Linux+networking + lab build. W2 OWASP Top 10 on Juice Shop + fix code. W3 Nmap/ZAP on own VMs + harden. W4 C/memory theory + compiler mitigations + fuzz own toy program. W5 Blue: Suricata+Wazuh alerts + IR drill. W6 Bounty-style report on lab target with fix PR. Throughout: ATT&CK mapping, write-ups, clean snapshots. Hack to protect. Learn stacks to build safer stacks. The best hacker on your network is the defender you trained.

let: Monkey Blog PT EN Índice Focados em problemas de Recuperação/Reparação Muitas ferramentas usadas para recuperar sectores de arranque, para Windows ou Linux, e muitas outras com ferramentas de esteganografia para investigar discos e ficheiros. Como funciona como o velho HirensBoot, de que gosto, é provável que aprove a distro Linux Leng Engineer Toolkit para usar conforme for preciso. Porque um sistema de recuperação ainda importa Um disco de recuperação resolve um problema que o computador moderno esconde muito bem: quando a máquina não arranca, não se pode pedir ajuda ao sistema operativo que está dentro do disco. Precisas de outro sistema, a correr de outro sítio, com ferramentas suficientes para olhar para o disco como um objecto em vez de um lugar onde vivem os teus ficheiros. É isso que é uma distribuição live. Não instala nada, não pede permissão, monta, inspecciona e reporta. O que está dentro desta Recuperação de sectores de arranque para Windows e Linux, que é a primeira coisa de que todos precisam e a última de que todos se lembram de preparar. Ferramentas para examinar um disco ao nível abaixo do sistema de ficheiros, onde uma partição apagada ainda é visível. E um conjunto de utilitários para dados escondidos, o tipo de trabalho que normalmente se chama forense quando é feito por um profissional e chama outra coisa quando é feito em casa. A comparação com o HirensBoot é justa. Aquele disco antigo tinha a mesma filosofia: pôr todas as ferramentas de que um técnico precisa num só lugar, arrancar de um CD e deixar de te preocupares com o sistema que se recusou a arrancar. A análise honesta Aprovo-a porque faz um trabalho e fá-lo sem um instalador a pedir que crie uma conta. Uma caixa de ferramentas devia ser aborrecida: arrancar, listar, montar, copiar, verificar, sair. Se ainda por cima for bonita, isso é um bónus, não uma funcionalidade. A única coisa que acrescentaria era uma página a dizer que ferramenta usar primeiro. Um disco cheio de utilitários é impressionante, mas às três da manhã o leitor precisa de um comando, não de um menu. Focused on Rescue/Repair problems Many tools used to recover boot sectors, for Windows or Linux and many other with steganos tools to investigate hard drivers and files. Since it works like the old HirensBoot, that I love it, I am likely to approve the Leng Engineer Toolkit Linux distro to use it as needed. Why a rescue system still matters A rescue disk solves a problem that the modern computer hides very well: when the machine does not boot, the operating system inside the disk cannot be asked for help. You need another system, running from somewhere else, with enough tools to look at the disk as an object instead of a place where your files live. That is what a live distribution is. It does not install anything, it does not ask permission, it mounts, inspects and reports. What is inside this one Recovery of boot sectors for Windows and Linux, which is the first thing everyone needs and the last thing everyone remembers to prepare. Tools to examine a disk at the level below the file system, where a deleted partition is still visible. And a set of utilities for hidden data, the kind of work that is usually called forensics when it is done by a professional and called something else when it is done at home. The comparison with HirensBoot is fair. That old disk had the same philosophy: put every tool a technician needs in one place, boot it from a CD, and stop worrying about the system that refused to start. The honest review I approve it because it does one job and does it without an installer asking me to create an account. A toolkit should be boring: boot, list, mount, copy, verify, leave. If it also looks nice, that is a bonus, not a feature. The only thing I would add is a page that says which tool to use first. A disk full of utilities is impressive, but at three in the morning the reader needs one command, not a menu.

lfs: LFS — Linux From Scratch: From Zero to a Booted OS You start with a running Linux host and an empty partition. You end with your own compiled Linux system that boots without the host. No installer, no package manager — every binary built by you, in order. Based on LFS 13.1-systemd (2026, kernel 7.1.8, GCC 16.2, glibc 2.44, Binutils 2.47) . Older stable: 12.4 . News: lfs/news . Overview: how LFS builds . Rules: follow ONE book version exactly — never mix versions. Backup the host. Disk names below ( /dev/sda ) are examples — use lsblk for yours. Full build takes 4–12h depending on CPU. 4 cores + 8GB RAM recommended. 1. What LFS Is (and Is Not) LFS is a recipe book , not a distro. It teaches: cross-toolchain → temp tools → chroot → final system → kernel → bootloader. You learn what a distro hides: how glibc talks to the kernel, why build order matters, what /tools isolation is for. LFS gives you LFS does NOT give you Minimal bootable systemd Linux, sources + patches Package manager, desktop, wifi wizard Deep understanding of toolchain Security updates automatically (you rebuild) Base for BLFS (desktop, server on top) Shortcuts — every package compiled in order After LFS comes BLFS (Beyond LFS) for X, desktop, network services. 2. Host Preparation Ref: host requirements . Host kernel ≥ 5.10, bash, gcc, binutils, bison, coreutils, make, perl, python3, etc. # Run the book's version-check script (download from book ch.2), then: bash version-check.sh # Must all pass. On Debian/Ubuntu, roughly: sudo apt install build-essential bison gawk m4 texinfo python3 libncurses-dev uname -r # >= 5.10 ? ls -l /bin/sh # must point to bash, NOT dash: sudo dpkg-reconfigure dash Host GCC newer than the book's (16.2) or binutils newer than 2.47 = untested . Prefer a host close to the book. First-timers: do NOT add custom CFLAGS — chapter 8 warns optimizations break builds. 3. Partition, Filesystem, Mount Ref: partitioning , filesystems . Need ≥10GB, 30GB comfortable, ~20GB sweet spot. ext4 default. UEFI needs ESP 128–256MB; BIOS+GPT needs BIOS Boot partition; optional 200MB /boot. lsblk # IDENTIFY your empty disk/partition first! sudo cfdisk /dev/sdb # example: sdb1 512M EFI (if UEFI), sdb2 30G Linux, sdb3 swap sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb2 sudo mkfs.vfat -F32 /dev/sdb1 # only if UEFI ESP sudo mkswap /dev/sdb3; sudo swapon /dev/sdb3 export LFS=/mnt/lfs # book convention — keep in every shell! sudo mkdir -pv $LFS; sudo mount -v -t ext4 /dev/sdb2 $LFS # Save it: echo "export LFS=/mnt/lfs" >> ~/.bashrc 4. Sources, Layout, lfs User sudo mkdir -v $LFS/sources; sudo chmod -v a+wt $LFS/sources # Download all tarballs + patches listed in book ch.3-4 (wget-list in book) sudo mkdir -pv $LFS/{etc,var,tools} $LFS/usr/{bin,lib,sbin} sudo groupadd lfs; sudo useradd -s /bin/bash -g lfs -m -k /dev/null lfs sudo chown -v lfs $LFS/{usr/*,lib,var,etc,bin,sbin,tools,sources} su - lfs cat > ~/.bash_profile ~/.bashrc Ref: lfs user . Building as lfs protects the host; root only where the book says. 5. Cross-Toolchain (Chapter 5) — Isolation From Host Goal: compiler that outputs for $LFS without linking host libs. Order matters: Binutils pass 1 → GCC pass 1 (limited, no full libc yet) → Linux headers → glibc → libstdc++. # Pattern for EVERY package (exact flags in book — copy them, don't improvise): tar xf binutils-2.47.tar.xz; cd binutils-2.47 mkdir -v build; cd build ../configure --prefix=$LFS/tools --with-sysroot=$LFS \ --target=$LFS_TGT --disable-nls --disable-werror make; make install; cd ../..; rm -rf binutils-2.47 build # Then GCC pass 1 (needs mpfr/gmp/mpc unpacked INSIDE gcc dir per book), # then: linux-7.1.8 headers 'make headers', then glibc 2.44, then libstdc++. # Sanity check after toolchain: echo 'int main(){}' | $LFS_TGT-gcc -xc - -v -o /tmp/a.out 2>&1 | grep -i sysroot Why two passes? Pass 1 builds with host help. Later (ch.6) Binutils/GCC pass 2 rebuild using the new libc inside $LFS — cutting the cord to the host. 6. Temporary Tools (Chapter 6) + Enter Chroot (Chapter 7) Ref: ch.6 intro . Cross-compile m4, ncurses, bash, coreutils, diffutils, file, findutils, gawk, grep, gzip, make, patch, sed, tar, xz, binutils pass 2, gcc pass 2 — installed under $LFS/tools and $LFS/usr . # As root (exit lfs user), mount virtual filesystems: sudo mount -v --bind /dev $LFS/dev sudo mount -vt devpts devpts $LFS/dev/pts -o gid=5,mode=0620 sudo mount -vt proc proc $LFS/proc sudo mount -vt sysfs sysfs $LFS/sys sudo mount -vt tmpfs shm $LFS/dev/shm # Then chroot — /tools/bin GONE from PATH now, target tools used: sudo chroot "$LFS" /usr/bin/env -i HOME=/root TERM="$TERM" \ PS1='(lfs chroot) \u:\w\$ ' PATH=/usr/bin:/usr/sbin /bin/bash --login # Ref: https://www.linuxfromscratch.org/lfs/view/13.1-systemd/chapter07/chroot.html # Inside: ch.7 temp tools + cleanup /tools. 7. Final System (Chapter 8) — The Real Build Ref: ch.8 intro , contents . ~70 packages in strict order: glibc (final) → binutils → gcc → … → systemd → grub. Each follows configure/make/test/install; run tests where book says (GCC/glibc tests take long but catch breakage). # Inside chroot, example rhythm (READ book flags per package!): tar xf glibc-2.44.tar.xz; cd glibc-2.44 mkdir -v build; cd build ../configure --prefix=/usr --disable-werror --enable-kernel=5.10 \ --enable-stack-protector=strong --disable-nscd libc_cv_slibdir=/usr/lib make; make check # expect some failures — book lists which are OK make install; cd ../..; rm -rf glibc-2.44 build # Continue per book: zlib, bzip2, xz, zstd, file, readline, m4, bc, flex, # binutils, gmp/mpfr/mpc, attr/acl, shadow, gcc (final), ncurses, sed, # psmisc, gettext, bison, grep, bash, libtool, gdbm, gperf, expat, inetutils, # less, perl, XML::Parser, intel-ucode?, libffi, openssl, python3, ninja, # meson, kmod, libelf, libffi, e2fsprogs, coreutils, ..., systemd, ..., grub. Common failures: skipped make check confusion (compare with book's expected fails), wrong timezone of errors from custom CFLAGS, running out of disk (need ~10GB free during gcc), /dev not mounted before udev/systemd steps. 8. System Configuration (Chapter 9) # fstab — ADAPT UUIDs (blkid): cat > /etc/fstab /etc/hostname passwd root ln -sfv /usr/share/zoneinfo/Europe/Lisbon /etc/localtime # systemd-networkd .network file per book; systemctl enable systemd-networkd systemd-resolved 9. Kernel + Bootloader (Chapter 10) → First Boot (Ch.11) Ref: kernel , grub . Disable Secure Boot (book procedure doesn't support it). # In chroot, /sources: tar xf linux-7.1.8.tar.xz; cd linux-7.1.8 make mrproper make defconfig; make menuconfig # MUST enable: your disk (AHCI/NVMe!), ext4, EFI stub if UEFI, SMP. make -j$(nproc); make modules_install cp -v arch/x86/boot/bzImage /boot/vmlinuz-7.1.8-lfs cp -v System.map /boot/System.map-7.1.8; cp -v .config /boot/config-7.1.8 # GRUB BIOS: grub-install /dev/sdb --target=i386-pc (whole disk, CAREFUL) # GRUB UEFI: mount ESP at /boot/efi, then: grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --removable cat > /boot/grub/grub.cfg /dev/null sudo reboot # select LFS disk in BIOS/UEFI Booted? Login as root → uname -a; systemctl status . You now run a self-built OS. Next: BLFS for networking extras, firmware, editor, SSH, desktop. 10. After Boot — Make It Usable & Safe # Inside new LFS: systemd-firstboot? # set locale/time/hostname if skipped useradd -m -G wheel andre; passwd andre # stop using root daily # BLFS next steps: linux-firmware, dhcpcd/NetworkManager, openssh, vim, curl, ca-certificates # Backups: dd or fsarchiver the partition BEFORE experimenting: # fsarchiver savefs /backup/lfs-clean.fsa /dev/sdb2 If this happens Do this Kernel panic: can't mount root Wrong root= name or missing disk/ext4 driver — rebuild kernel with AHCI/NVMe + ext4 built-in (not modules) GRUB rescue> Boot live USB, mount, re-run grub-install with right --target + fix grub.cfg paths No network Missing NIC driver/firmware — lspci from host, enable driver, add linux-firmware via BLFS Build fails at package X Re-read that page: missed dep? wrong user (lfs vs root vs chroot)? clean src dir and retry exactly Sources: LFS news, 13.1-systemd book ch.1/2/4/5/6/7/8/10, kernel+grub pages, BLFS project — all linked above.
liberdade: Saltar para o conteúdo Consciência e liberdade A− A+ Imprimir Ensaio · liberdade de consciência O direito de não viver sob vigilância Uma sociedade livre protege a associação, a privacidade e a experimentação social — sem transformar a discrição em suspeita automática, nem a crítica política em licença para causar dano. Defender espaços reservados para movimentos pacíficos não é defender o crime: é defender que a liberdade de consciência também inclui escolher quando, como e perante quem se tornam públicas as nossas ideias. 1. Consciência, escolha e senso comum A consciência é a capacidade de formar juízos, rever convicções e orientar a própria vida. Dela decorrem liberdades fundamentais: pensar, expressar opiniões, associar-se, recusar uma participação e procurar modos diferentes de organizar a comunidade. O senso comum acrescenta uma regra prática: a liberdade de cada pessoa deve coexistir com a segurança e a liberdade das outras. Por isso, proteger a autonomia não significa aceitar qualquer conduta. Significa exigir razões concretas antes de restringir escolhas e distinguir uma ideia incómoda de um dano demonstrável. Uma alternativa económica ou social pode desafiar interesses instalados e, ainda assim, ser pacífica e legítima. 2. Discrição não é sinónimo de crime Um grupo pode optar por não divulgar a identidade dos seus membros, as suas conversas ou todos os pormenores da sua organização. Pode fazê-lo para evitar assédio, discriminação, represálias ou apropriação das suas ideias. A reserva — e até uma forma de clandestinidade entendida como existência fora da exposição pública — não prova, por si só, qualquer atividade ilícita. O princípio deve ser o mesmo para todos: julgar atos e provas, não presumir culpa a partir da falta de publicidade. A exposição pública pode colocar pessoas e iniciativas em risco, pelo que a transparência não deve ser imposta sem ponderar necessidade, proporcionalidade e salvaguardas. Isso não equivale a afirmar que toda a divulgação termina necessariamente com um movimento; significa reconhecer que ela pode ter custos reais. Uma fronteira necessária: defender o direito à privacidade e à associação pacífica não é fornecer meios para escapar à investigação, esconder violência ou impedir a responsabilização por danos. 3. Espaço para alternativas sociais e económicas Cooperativas, redes de apoio mútuo, escolas livres e outras experiências comunitárias podem propor respostas diferentes às hierarquias do mercado e do Estado. O seu valor deve ser avaliado pelo que fazem: se respeitam o consentimento, se protegem quem participa e se não prejudicam terceiros — não apenas por desafiarem o grande capital, um governo ou a norma dominante. Uma Escola Livre que não agride nem explora terceiros merece debate e avaliação justa, não suspeição automática. A liberdade de criar alternativas inclui o direito de as organizar com discrição, respeitando os deveres legais aplicáveis e os direitos de crianças, famílias, trabalhadores e comunidade. 4. Política de drogas: reduzir dano e proteger consentimento A palavra “tráfico” agrega realidades distintas e, por si só, não descreve consentimento, composição do produto ou violência. Como proposta de reforma — e não como descrição da lei em vigor — é possível defender que a resposta penal se concentre prioritariamente em danos concretos, coerção e violência, em vez de punir automaticamente o consumo ou toda a circulação de substâncias. Nesta perspetiva, três linhas de gravidade merecem atenção especial: Consumo forçado: administrar ou impor uma substância sem consentimento viola a autonomia e exige proteção da pessoa afetada. Produto adulterado de forma perigosa ou fraudulenta: ocultar a composição ou criar risco sério para a saúde justifica uma resposta firme e proporcional. Armas e violência letal: o uso de armas, ameaças ou homicídio transforma uma transação ou conflito numa ameaça direta à vida e à segurança de terceiros. Esta proposta não resolve, por si só, questões de saúde pública, proteção de menores, qualidade e informação sobre produtos, dependência ou exploração económica. Uma política responsável teria de as enfrentar com evidência, prevenção, redução de danos e acesso a cuidados, sem fingir que a simples descriminalização elimina todos os riscos. 5. Armas, consciência e responsabilidade Quem empunha uma arma de fogo sabe — ou tem o dever de saber — que o seu uso pode ferir ou matar. A consciência previsível das consequências aumenta o dever de contenção; não torna, por si só, todo o uso da arma um crime. A avaliação depende do contexto, da lei aplicável, da necessidade, da proporcionalidade e dos factos. linuxDistroComparison: Linux Field Manual · Distribution Atlas Linux Distributions, Compared Every Linux distribution ships the same kernel and runs the same applications, and yet the experience of using Debian, Fedora, Arch and NixOS is completely different. The differences are not in the programs: they are in who decides what gets installed , when the system changes , and what happens when it breaks . This is a reference to what each family actually does, what it is for, and how the distros inside a family differ from each other. Before the catalogue, one definition worth carrying: a distribution is kernel + userland + package manager + release policy + installer + support model. The desktop environment is a layer on top (GNOME, KDE Plasma and Xfce are available almost everywhere), and the C library and init system are quietly decisive for compatibility. If you remember the four questions — fixed or rolling, who packages, what breaks, who supports — most of the distro debate answers itself. For a broader tour of reviews and experiments on this blog, see Some Distros that look different , Hard to maintain , Almighty Linux Short Review and Overkill & HardenWing . The two axes that explain everything Release model. A fixed distribution freezes a set of package versions, tests them together, and ships a release you can keep for years. A rolling distribution updates continuously: you install once and receive new versions as they are packaged. Fixed means predictable and slow to change; rolling means current and occasionally surprising. There is no third option that escapes this trade-off — every "curated rolling" distro is just rolling with an extra delay. Package policy. The second axis is who decides what enters the system and how. Binary package managers (APT, DNF, pacman, zypper, xbps, apk) install pre-built packages. Source-based systems (Portage) compile locally and let you choose options per package. Declarative systems (Nix) build the whole system from a description and keep every previous generation on disk. A distribution is, more than anything else, a policy about change. Two technical layers matter downstream: libc (glibc almost everywhere, musl on Alpine and optional on Void/Gentoo) and init (systemd almost everywhere, OpenRC on Alpine and Gentoo by default, runit on Void, sysvinit-style scripts on Devuan and Slackware). Most incompatibilities people blame on "the distro" are really glibc/musl or systemd assumptions. Debian and its children The Debian family is the largest ecosystem in Linux, and its defining property is patience. Debian's stable branch freezes for roughly two years, receives security support for about three, and can be extended further by the LTS team. Packages are built against a single policy document, the social contract keeps the system free, and the result is the distro people install on servers they intend to forget about. Ubuntu, Mint, Kali, MX and dozens of others are variations on this base. Debian The reference implementation of stable Linux. Three branches — stable, testing, unstable (sid) — with APT on top. Conservative versions, excellent documentation, no corporate owner, and a community that argues about governance for sport. APT · fixed · systemd · glibc Ubuntu Debian-based, six-month releases and a two-year LTS cadence with five years of standard support (extendable commercially). Adds Snaps, PPAs and its own tooling. The default choice for cloud images and third-party software instructions. APT + Snap · fixed · systemd · glibc Linux Mint Ubuntu LTS base (or Debian, in LMDE) with Cinnamon, MATE or Xfce. Removes Snaps by default, ships a cautious update manager and tools that assume the user should not have to read a wiki to install a printer. APT · fixed · systemd · glibc Pop!_OS System76's Ubuntu LTS derivative, built for their hardware and for people who want a polished desktop without configuration. Adds a recovery partition and its own COSMIC desktop work. APT · fixed · systemd · glibc Kali Linux Debian-based rolling release with hundreds of security tools. It is a toolkit, not a daily driver: the default configuration is deliberately permissive for testing, and using it as a main system trades stability for tool availability. APT · rolling · systemd · glibc MX Linux Debian stable with Xfce, its own MX Tools and systemd optional by default. A pragmatic desktop for older hardware and for users who want Debian without assembling the pieces. APT · fixed · sysvinit/systemd · glibc Debian's children differ mostly in defaults and support politics : Ubuntu brings commercial support and newer software; Mint removes Snaps and targets desktop users; Kali inverts the security defaults; MX preserves Debian's stability with a friendlier toolset. The package manager is identical, which is why skills transfer. For the Debian view on this blog, see Debian Forever , Debian, simple and fast , an introduction to APT , and the Debian technical manual for the boot-to-security walkthrough. The Red Hat family Red Hat's world is defined by enterprise support and by SELinux. Fedora is the fast-moving community project where the technology is developed; RHEL is the slow, certified, subscription product; Rocky and Alma rebuild RHEL without the subscription; CentOS Stream sits upstream of RHEL as its rolling preview. All use RPM packaging with DNF and default to SELinux enforcing — the single biggest practical difference from the Debian family after corporate support. Both halves of that stack have a manual on this blog: the RHEL technical manual walks the administration track from install to automation, and SELinux, zero to hero goes through contexts, type enforcement and the policy tools. Fedora Six-month releases with about thirteen months of support each. New kernels, new GNOME, new Wayland — first. SELinux enforcing, DNF5, and atomic variants (Silverblue) that treat the OS as an image. DNF · fixed · systemd · SELinux RHEL The commercial distribution: ten-year life cycles, certifications, vendor support and predictable backports. You pay for the support contract, not for the software bits. DNF · fixed · systemd · SELinux Rocky Linux A community, bug-for-bug rebuild of RHEL, created after CentOS pivoted to Stream. Same ABI, same packages, no subscription. DNF · fixed · systemd · SELinux AlmaLinux The other RHEL rebuild, backed by CloudLinux. Functionally interchangeable with Rocky for most workloads; the choice usually comes down to governance and funding. DNF · fixed · systemd · SELinux CentOS Stream Rolling preview of the next RHEL minor release. Good for testing and CI against what RHEL will become; not a drop-in replacement for the old stable CentOS people remember. DNF · rolling · systemd · SELinux openSUSE and SUSE openSUSE is the community arm of SUSE, and its distinguishing features are YaST (a system administration tool that predates most of the competition), the zypper package manager, and Btrfs snapshots wired into the bootloader. Leap is the fixed, enterprise-aligned release; Tumbleweed is a rolling distribution with automated testing before each snapshot. When an upgrade goes wrong, the rollback is a boot menu entry — the most underrated safety net in the Linux world. openSUSE Leap Fixed releases built from SUSE Linux Enterprise sources. Excellent for workstations and small servers where you want stability plus YaST's centralised configuration. zypper · fixed · systemd · glibc openSUSE Tumbleweed Rolling, but with openQA testing every snapshot and automatic Btrfs snapshots. The most conservative way to run a rolling distribution. zypper · rolling · systemd · glibc Arch and its derivatives Arch is a philosophy as much as a distribution: minimal base install, no defaults you did not choose, rolling packages, and the Arch Wiki — arguably the best Linux documentation ever written, useful even on other distros. pacman is fast and simple; the AUR supplies user-maintained build scripts for almost everything else. The cost is that you assemble the system and you own the breakage. Manjaro and EndeavourOS package the same base with different amounts of hand-holding. Arch Linux Rolling, minimal, and explicit: you install what you need, read the wiki, and learn how the system fits together. archinstall now provides a guided installer without changing the philosophy. pacman · rolling · systemd · glibc Manjaro Arch packages held back for extra testing, plus its own tools for kernels, drivers and updates. A friendlier on-ramp that occasionally creates its own compatibility puzzles. pacman + pamac · rolling · systemd · glibc EndeavourOS An Arch installer and a sensible default setup with a small theme layer. Nearly vanilla Arch, without the manual partitioning ritual. pacman · rolling · systemd · glibc The independents These distributions do not share a base with the families above, and that is the point: each one is an argument about how a system should be built. Gentoo argues for compilation and choice; NixOS argues for reproducibility and rollback; Slackware argues for simplicity and tradition; Void argues for minimalism without systemd; Alpine argues for small and secure, which is why it runs inside so many containers. Below all of them sits Linux From Scratch , which is not a distribution at all but the recipe distributions are made from: it builds the toolchain, the C library and the kernel by hand, and it is the fastest way to see what every entry in the table below is actually hiding. Gentoo Source-based: Portage compiles packages with the options you select in USE flags. Maximum control and optimisation, paid for in compile time and maintenance attention. OpenRC by default, systemd optional, musl supported. Portage · rolling · OpenRC · glibc/musl NixOS The entire system is a declarative configuration. Upgrades are atomic, every generation stays bootable, and rolling back is selecting an older entry. The learning curve is the price of never having a half-upgraded machine. Nix · rolling · systemd · glibc Slackware The oldest maintained distribution, still shipping a clean, traditional system with BSD-style init scripts and no dependency resolution. You learn what every package does because you install every package. slackpkg · fixed · sysvinit · glibc Void Linux Rolling, lightweight, with runit instead of systemd and the xbps package manager. A clean middle ground between Arch's freshness and a minimal init. xbps · rolling · runit · glibc/musl Alpine Linux musl libc, BusyBox userland, OpenRC, and a whole system measured in megabytes. The default base image for containers; usable as a desktop, unusual as one. apk · fixed/edge · OpenRC · musl One table to compare them all Distribution Base Package manager Release Init Libc Best for Debian independent APT fixed systemd glibc servers, stability Ubuntu LTS Debian APT, Snap fixed systemd glibc general use, cloud Linux Mint Ubuntu/Debian APT fixed systemd glibc desktop beginners Pop!_OS Ubuntu APT fixed systemd glibc creators, System76 Kali Debian APT rolling systemd glibc security testing MX Linux Debian APT fixed sysvinit/systemd glibc older hardware Fedora independent DNF fixed (short) systemd glibc new tech, developers RHEL independent DNF fixed (10 y) systemd glibc enterprise Rocky / Alma RHEL DNF fixed (10 y) systemd glibc free RHEL CentOS Stream RHEL upstream DNF rolling preview systemd glibc CI for RHEL openSUSE Leap SUSE zypper fixed systemd glibc workstations, servers Tumbleweed openSUSE zypper rolling systemd glibc safe rolling Arch independent pacman rolling systemd glibc control, learning Manjaro Arch pacman/pamac rolling (delayed) systemd glibc easy Arch EndeavourOS Arch pacman rolling systemd glibc near-vanilla Arch Gentoo independent Portage rolling OpenRC/systemd glibc/musl control, compilation NixOS independent Nix rolling systemd glibc reproducibility Slackware independent slackpkg fixed sysvinit glibc tradition Void independent xbps rolling runit glibc/musl minimalism Alpine independent apk fixed/edge OpenRC musl containers The differences that actually bite Upgrades A fixed distribution upgrades in steps: do-release-upgrade , dnf system-upgrade , or a new ISO and a migration plan. A rolling distribution upgrades continuously, which means a broken update can arrive on a Tuesday. Arch and NixOS both make rollback practical — snapshots or generations — and that safety net changes the risk calculus more than the version numbers do. Security models Fedora, RHEL and friends default to SELinux enforcing (the SELinux manual covers what that means in practice). Debian and Ubuntu default to AppArmor, enabled for common services. Alpine and Gentoo are minimal by default and leave the hardening to you. This matters far more than the wallpaper: two systems with the same applications can have completely different mandatory access controls. Stability versus freshness Debian stable and RHEL will not give you the newest compiler, and that is a feature: the system is tested as a whole. Arch and Tumbleweed will give you the newest everything, with the understanding that you are part of the testing. Fedora sits in the middle: new technology, predictable short lifecycles. The honest question is not "which is better" but "how much change can my workflow absorb this month". The same runtime, packaged differently Python ships on nearly every distribution, and it is the clearest case of packaging policy reaching the user. Debian and Ubuntu mark the system interpreter as externally managed (PEP 668), so pip install refuses to touch it and points you at a virtual environment; Fedora tracks recent versions closely and expects the same discipline; Arch is normally on the newest release; Alpine builds against musl, where many binary wheels do not exist and packages get compiled locally. None of this is a Python problem — it is the distribution's policy surfacing in your terminal. For the long version, from installing Python without wrecking the system to running it in production, see the Python 3 field manual . Licensing, governance and money Debian is a community project with a constitution. Ubuntu, RHEL and SUSE have commercial parents whose interests sometimes diverge from users' (Snaps, subscriptions, licensing changes). Rocky and Alma exist precisely because a licensing decision changed a community's plans. Choose a distro with a governance model you are willing to live with, because that model decides what happens in a decade. musl versus glibc Alpine's small size comes from musl, and musl is not binary-compatible with glibc. Some pre-built software — including some proprietary tools and language runtimes — simply will not run. This is fine for containers and Go binaries; it is a daily annoyance on a desktop. Void and Gentoo expose the choice explicitly, which is the honest way to present it. Which one should you install? Profile Reasonable choice Why First Linux desktop Linux Mint or Ubuntu LTS Hardware support, documentation, and a desktop that behaves. Developer who wants current tools Fedora or Arch Recent compilers and runtimes; Fedora with more guardrails, Arch with more control. Server that must not surprise you Debian stable or RHEL/Rocky Long support, conservative updates, boring in the best sense. Enterprise with vendor contracts RHEL or SUSE Certification and support are the product. Rolling with a safety net openSUSE Tumbleweed Snapshots and automated testing around a rolling base. Reproducible infrastructure NixOS Declarative configuration and atomic rollback. Containers and tiny images Alpine Small, secure defaults, musl trade-off accepted. Learning how Linux works Arch or Gentoo You build it, therefore you understand it. Old laptop, limited RAM MX Linux, Void or Alpine Lightweight defaults without a modern desktop tax. No distribution matches that search. Try a shorter term or another profile. One honest caveat to finish: the distro matters less than the internet believes . The same Firefox, the same Python, the same Flatpak applications and the same containers run everywhere. What changes is package policy, support horizon, defaults and the community you will ask for help. Pick the policy you can live with, learn its package manager properly, and stop distro-hopping when the system starts working. That is usually the moment the operating system becomes boring — and boring is the goal. lutaDoPoderNaRealidade: Ensaio · poder real, não mito de poder A Luta do Poder na Realidade Quem manda, quem mantém, quem disfarça, quem coloca o questionamento no chão: um olhar sobre a luta do poder na realidade, e sobre a cor que um treinador filosófico usa para disfarçar o que ele diria de outra forma. calor chumbo distanciador descer Nota de entrada sobre o que é real, já — e o que esses números não dizem Há uma espécie de conversa que o poder não tolera tanto quanto o riso ou a dúvida: é a conversa em que alguém pergunta o que é que o poder está a fazer, em termos que o poder não tenha preparada uma resposta elegante. A luta do poder na realidade não é, quase nunca, o que se conta nos filmes de génio de género. Não é o grito no palácio, nem o golpe que “resolve tudo”, nem a mão invisível que desvia o destino com um gesto sutil. É mais lento do que isso, e mais cansativo. É quem mantém a conversa aberta, quem faz a pergunta desaparecer do centro da atenção, quem decide se o que se chama “problema” é um problema ou apenas um incómodo em quem o nomeou. Neste ensaio não se trata de tirar o poder dos outros como se fosse um objecto que se pode apanhar. Trata-se de ver o que é que o poder, de facto, faz, e o que é que ele deixa de fazer quando se transforma em cor. Também não é escrito como se o leitor não tivesse números próprios para comparar: há relatórios, há organogramas, há nomes de departamentos, há centros de prova e tabelas de espetadores. Quando a cor entra nessa realidade, o conflito não desaparece — e pode valer a pena ler os mesmos dados que lêem quem mantém o assunto no sentido que interessa. 1 · O que é o poder de um modo que não adolescente O poder é, primeiramente, uma relação. Não um monopólio de força, nem uma coleção de títulos, e menos ainda uma qualidade que se tem ou não se tem — como se fosse sangue, ou cor, ou genialidade. Se fosse isso, bastava um exame de sangue para explicar as hierarquias. Há aqui um ponto que nem sempre se diz abertamente em português: a distinção entre o poder real e o poder reportável. O poder real é esse que aparece nas coisas que acontecem depois — nas horas perdidas, nos termos em que se escreve, nos nomes que se repetem, nos défices que ninguém suaviza. O poder reportável é outro: o que cai num organograma, numa audiência pública, num relatório de região fiscal, num artigo de revista, num documento que usa as cores certas para parecer imune ao duvidar. E é exatamente sobre essa segunda camada — e sobre o que ela deixa de fora — que este ensaio aperta. O que está longe mais frequentemente é a capacidade de continuar no assunto depois de haver vontade em o abandonar. Uma pergunta que não é respondida, mas desviada. Um incómodo que não é removido, mas reclassificado. Uma mudança de tom de voz que não é impressa no minuto a seguir, mas que altera a distância entre quem fala e quem ouve. Isso é o poder real: não o comando direto, que é a forma óbvia; é a forma disfarçada de decisão tardia, que parece apenas um estilo, um temperamento, uma personalidade. Parece “assunto de quem está lá”, mas muitas vezes é apenas “assunto da cor que é fácil de manter no ar”. 2 · Como o poder se mantém não apenas com a mão firme Um poder que depende só da força é um poder que gasta energia demais. A força bruta consome quem a usa — ou ao menos consome o repouso, o tempo, a atenção. Uma instituição, uma família, um parceiro, um grupo de colegas, um Estado: a forma de poder que se sustenta não é apenas a que grita, é a que pode dispensar o grito e ainda assim deixar a conversa nos mesmos termos. Isso se faz com três gestos reiterados, que se confundem frequentemente com coisas diferentes: Tempo. Quem demora, desgasta. Não porque o argumento se exaure, mas porque a atenção e a paciência têm um fim ao lado da razão. Distorção de classificação. Um incómodo passa a ser “demais sensível”, “excessivo”, “desrespeitoso”, “sem maturidade”. O objecto da luta muda de categoria sem passar por porta. Cor no rosto do assunto. Se a coisa que se discute ganha uma cor que torna o discurso mais fácil, mais agradável, mais “sabio”, então o poder não precisa mesmo de excluir: precisa apenas de pintar de outra maneira — muitas vezes com linguagem de organogramas, com exportações controladas, com discurso que já foi aprovado em outra sala. Nenhum deles é, por si só, um crime. Todos juntos são uma forma de dirigir quem está a lutar. E é sobre este terceiro gesto — sobre a cor — que este ensaio fica mais tempo, porque é a que mais facilmente se confunde com inteligência. 3 · Cor de coaching filosófico quando parece desenhar e na verdade desvia Há uma cor, num coaching que se apresenta como filosófico, que não é apenas paleta. É um comportamento que se disfarça de sensibilidade. Chama-se de “ria”, de “pleno”, de “calmo”, de “regional”, de “natural”; no fim, chama-se de algo que as pessoas acham difícil de contradizer sem desequilíbrio. A cor, aqui, é literal e também não: é a atmosfera que um discurso cria para si próprio, e a razão pela qual o discurso parece mais sábio do que teria sido com outra cor.
